stimulus.text:
“Without some alteration in our political creed, the superstructure we have been seven years raising at the expence of much blood and treasure, must fall. We are fast verging to anarchy and confusion! . . . Thirteen sovereignties pulling against each other, and all tugging at the Federal head, will soon bring ruin on the whole; whereas a liberal and energetic Constitution, well guarded and closely watched, to prevent encroachments, might restore us to that degree of respectability and consequence, to which we are entitled.”

—George Washington to James Madison, Mount Vernon, November 5, 1786
stimulus.source_note: George Washington to James Madison, Mount Vernon, November 5, 1786. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — George Washington to James Madison, Mount Vernon, November 5, 1786, public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification

primary_sources: George Washington to James Madison, November 5, 1786

stem: In this letter, what remedy does Washington call for?

options.text: A return to rule by the British crown
options.misconception: Washington led the war for independence; he never called for a return to British rule.

options.text: A league of states with no central government at all
options.misconception: A league with no center is what the Articles already were, and Washington says that system is failing.

options.text: A bill of rights to limit the power of the states
options.misconception: The letter never mentions a bill of rights; its remedy is a stronger frame of government.

options.text: A liberal and energetic Constitution, well guarded against encroachments

rationales.D: Washington's own words name the remedy: a liberal and energetic Constitution, well guarded and closely watched, to prevent encroachments.
rationales.A: Background: Washington fought for independence, so a return to British rule is the opposite of his position.
rationales.B: Background: the Articles already were a loose league, and Washington says that arrangement is verging on anarchy.
rationales.C: No bill of rights appears in the letter; Washington's remedy is a stronger Constitution.
rationales.general:
1. Washington says the superstructure built since independence must fall without an alteration.
2. The alteration he names is a liberal and energetic Constitution.
3. He adds a guard: it must be well guarded and closely watched, to prevent encroachments.
4. The other choices miss his words: no return to Britain, no league with no center, and no bill of rights in this letter.
Remember: when a writer names his own remedy, use his words, not yours.
